passage: Three weeks after Xin told the whole robotics club that Emil had cried at his grandfather's funeral, Emil still walked the long way round their Vancouver school so he wouldn't pass her locker. At lunch he said, "Honestly, I don't even care any more," and laughed too loudly. That night he found their old shared playlist and couldn't stop scrolling: songs from bus rides, the silly one they sang at the science fair. His chest ached. At breakfast his mother noticed his untouched toast. Emil stared at the table. "I miss her. Not what she did. Her. It's like someone died, but she's still in my maths class." His mother sat down beside him. "That's grief. It makes sense." Saying it out loud didn't fix anything, but his shoulders came down.

qa.q: What did Xin tell the robotics club?
qa.a: Xin told them that Emil had cried at his grandfather's funeral.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling as he scrolled through the old playlist?
qa.a: Emil felt grief and loss for the friendship, an ache in his chest that his "I don't care" laugh had hidden.

qa.q: Why did saying "I miss her" help more than "I don't care"?
qa.a: Naming the grief out loud let his mother recognise it and comfort him, while pretending not to care kept the ache hidden.

qa.q: How might Xin experience Emil walking the long way round her locker?
qa.a: Xin may feel guilty and shut out, sensing she has lost her best friend.

grounding: Illustrates a teen mourning a friendship lost to a betrayed secret, and how naming the grief helps more than pretending not to care.

passage: In the girls' hostel in Dehradun, Rukmini moved her bed to the far end of the dorm after Rekha read her poem notebook aloud to the others. They had shared a study table for three years. Now they passed in the mess without a word. Rukmini told everyone she was fine, busier and happier than ever. But on Sunday evening she sat on the steps behind the laundry and cried until her nose ran. The warden, Mrs Negi, found her there and sat on the step below. "You've lost your closest friend. That's a real loss, even if she's still here." Rukmini nodded. "I keep turning round to tell her things." "Then let yourself be sad about it for a while," Mrs Negi said. "Pretending costs more."

qa.q: How long had Rukmini and Rekha shared a study table?
qa.a: They had shared a study table for three years.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling on the steps behind the laundry?
qa.a: Rukmini felt deep sadness and grief for the lost friendship, which she had been hiding by acting fine.

qa.q: How did Mrs Negi help Rukmini?
qa.a: Mrs Negi named the loss as real and gave Rukmini permission to be sad instead of pretending.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Rukmini moving her bed to the far end?
qa.a: Rekha may feel the distance as a sharp punishment, and perhaps regret, realising how much she broke.

grounding: Shows a teen grieving a best friendship broken by a betrayed secret, and an adult helping her name the grief instead of pretending.

passage:
"Santosh Sir, may I talk to you about my project mark?"
"The mark is final, Ayesha. You submitted late."
"I understand, Sir. I just want to show you something." She held out her phone. "The upload page crashed at 11:52. Here's the screenshot of the error, and my email to you at 11:55 with the file attached."
"Hmm."
"Five other students had the same error. Meena and Joel have screenshots too."
"Why didn't you raise it at the time?"
"I did, in the email. I think it went to spam."
"Let me check with the IT office. If this is right, I'll correct all six marks."
"Thank you, Sir. And if the IT office can't confirm it, could we ask the coordinator?"
"Fair. Come by on Friday."

qa.q: At what time did the upload page crash?
qa.a: The upload page crashed at 11:52.

qa.q: What might Ayesha have been feeling when she first asked about her mark?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt nervous and wronged, but determined to be heard fairly.

qa.q: What made Ayesha's dissent effective?
qa.a: She stayed polite, brought evidence like the screenshot and email, named others affected and suggested the coordinator as a proper channel.

qa.q: How does Santosh Sir see the screenshot?
qa.a: Santosh Sir seems to see it as fair evidence that makes him rethink, which is why he agrees to check with the IT office.

grounding: Illustrates a teen raising a concern about an unfair mark politely, with evidence and a proper channel.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and last term I learned this the hard way. Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team, even when Ira and I had higher scores in the trials. For a month I said nothing and just sulked. Nothing changed. Then one day I snapped in class: "You only pick your favourites!" The room went silent, and I got sent out. That didn't help either. Ira suggested another way. We collected the trial score sheets, wrote a short, polite letter asking how selection worked, and took it to the English coordinator. Two weeks later the school put up clear selection rules on the notice board. I made the team in the next round. I still cringe about snapping, though.

qa.q: Who kept picking the same four students?
qa.a: Mrs Rao kept picking the same four students for the debate team.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling during the month of saying nothing?
qa.a: Kavitha felt resentful and unfairly treated, sulking because the higher trial scores seemed ignored.

qa.q: Which approach finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Collecting the score sheets and taking a polite letter to the English coordinator used evidence and a proper channel, so the rules became clear.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt when Kavitha snapped in class?
qa.a: Mrs Rao probably felt accused and embarrassed in front of everyone, which made her less open to the complaint.

grounding: Shows a teen learning that silence and disrespect both fail against a seemingly unfair teacher, while evidence and a proper channel work.

passage: In their village outside Rohtak, Sharmila had covered one whole wall with newspaper cuttings of Raj Rani, the district's wrestling champion. So when a new billboard went up at the bus stand showing Raj Rani selling a skin-whitening cream, Sharmila was the first to defend it. "She needs money for training. She can do no wrong." Her cousin Sangeeta, home from college, raised an eyebrow. "You're dark like me. Does that ad make you feel good?" Sharmila opened her mouth, then shut it. She thought of the girls at school who were teased about their skin. That evening she didn't take down a single cutting. But in the margin of one she wrote: "Best on the mat. Wrong about this."

qa.q: Where did the new billboard go up?
qa.a: The billboard went up at the bus stand.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when she opened her mouth and then shut it?
qa.a: Sharmila felt uncomfortable and conflicted, seeing that the ad might hurt girls like her even though she loved Raj Rani.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's note in the margin show about healthy admiration?
qa.a: It shows Sharmila can keep admiring Raj Rani's wrestling while openly disagreeing with the ad, seeing her as human.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Sharmila's first defence?
qa.a: Sangeeta seems concerned that Sharmila is excusing something harmful out of hero worship, so she asks a gentle question.

grounding: Shows a teen who defends everything her sporting idol does learning to keep her admiration while disagreeing with one act.

passage:
Thursday night
I can't believe it. Dolma sent me the article at lunch: Meher Qadir, the climate speaker I've followed for two years, copied big parts of her famous river speech from a college student's blog. She even admitted it. I felt like someone punched me. Her quote is stuck above my desk. I was so upset I didn't eat dinner, and Ammi thought I was ill.
But after dinner I looked at the jute bag I made, and the neem saplings on our balcony. Meher didn't grow those. I did. The ideas still work even if she's not perfect. Tomorrow I'm replacing her quote with one from the student she copied.
Zeenat

qa.q: What did Meher Qadir copy?
qa.a: She copied big parts of her famous river speech from a college student's blog.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling after reading the article Dolma sent?
qa.a: Zeenat felt crushed and upset, as if punched, because the speaker followed for two years had copied.

qa.q: How did Zeenat keep the ideas while dropping the idolisation?
qa.a: Zeenat focused on the jute bag and neem saplings Zeenat made, and chose to honour the student who was copied.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen Zeenat skipping dinner?
qa.a: Ammi thought Zeenat was ill, not knowing the upset came from losing faith in a hero.

grounding: Illustrates a teen crushed when an admired speaker proves flawed, keeping the ideas while letting go of the idolisation.

passage: At the district athletics club, only one boy from the under-17 group would be picked for the state 800 metres. Sachin's rival, Tarun, beat him by two seconds in every trial. In the changing room someone joked, "Hide Tarun's spikes before Saturday." Sachin didn't laugh. He asked Coach Usha for Tarun's split times. "You want to copy him?" she asked. "I want to know where he's faster." The numbers showed it: the last 200 metres. For three weeks Sachin stayed after practice doing hill sprints until his legs shook. On selection day he lost by half a second. He shook Tarun's hand, then asked Coach Usha, "Next season?" She smiled. "Next season."

qa.q: By how much did Tarun beat Sachin in every trial?
qa.a: Tarun beat him by two seconds in every trial.

qa.q: Why didn't Sachin laugh at the joke about hiding Tarun's spikes?
qa.a: Sachin felt determined to beat Tarun fairly on the track, and sabotage felt wrong to him.

qa.q: How did Sachin use Tarun as a benchmark?
qa.a: He studied Tarun's split times, found the gap in the last 200 metres and trained it with hill sprints.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Sachin's handshake after selection?
qa.a: Tarun likely feels respected, and aware that Sachin will push him hard next season.

grounding: Illustrates a teen competing for a place by training harder and using the rival as a benchmark, without sabotage.

passage:
Hi Jyoti,

I know it's strange getting an email from me. We're both trying out for the one spot on the state debate team on the 14th, and I'll be honest: you're the person I'm most scared of. Your rebuttals are faster than anyone's in our school.

Somebody in my class said I should tell the judges you had help writing your speeches. I'm not doing that. It isn't true, and I don't want to win like that.

What I'd like instead: would you do three practice rounds with me after school next week? You'd get a sparring partner, and I'd get to see how you think on your feet. May the better speaker win.

Neelam

qa.q: When are Neelam and Jyoti trying out for the state debate team?
qa.a: They are both trying out for the one spot on the 14th.

qa.q: What is Neelam feeling about competing with Jyoti?
qa.a: Neelam feels scared of and admiring toward Jyoti's fast rebuttals, but determined to compete fairly.

qa.q: What makes Neelam's plan a healthy way to compete?
qa.a: Neelam refuses to spread the rumour and suggests practice rounds, using Jyoti as a benchmark to improve.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel reading the email?
qa.a: Jyoti may be surprised and a bit flattered, and could respect Neelam for choosing fair rivalry over rumours.

grounding: Shows a teen competing for one place by treating the rival as a benchmark and refusing to spread rumours.

passage: There was one district scholarship seat for their kasba school, and everyone knew it was between Jeevan and Zeenat. Jeevan couldn't stop thinking about her. He checked her test marks before his own, lay awake counting how many sums she'd done, and on the bus he watched her revise instead of revising himself. One afternoon he found her physics notebook left on a bench and held it a second too long, imagining it gone. His hands felt dirty. He put it back on her desk. That night he couldn't sleep again, and his mock-test score dropped by twelve marks. His grandfather, mending a net on the veranda, said, "You're running her race, not yours." Jeevan turned his desk to face the wall and made a timetable with no Zeenat in it.

qa.q: By how many marks did Jeevan's mock-test score drop?
qa.a: His mock-test score dropped by twelve marks.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he held Zeenat's notebook a second too long?
qa.a: Jeevan felt a pull of jealousy and then shame, as if his hands were dirty for even imagining it gone.

qa.q: What change helped Jeevan get back to his own growth?
qa.a: Turning his desk to the wall and making a timetable with no Zeenat in it put his energy into his own study.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel if she knew how closely Jeevan watched her?
qa.a: Zeenat might feel uneasy and pressured, since she is simply revising for the same seat.

grounding: Illustrates a teen fixated on defeating a rival, losing sleep and marks, and recognising the obsession drains his own growth.

passage: Leila had watched every one of Nkechi's netball clips from last season, pausing on her footwork until 1 a.m. The Birmingham under-16 team had one spot for goal attack, and Nkechi was her only real rival. Leila started noticing everything: who Nkechi sat with, what she ate, whether the coach smiled at her. She even drafted a message to the team group hinting that Nkechi had skipped fitness tests, then deleted it, ashamed. At Thursday's practice Leila dropped three easy passes because her eyes were on Nkechi instead of the ball. On the bus home her friend Grace said, "You play against her more than you play the game." Leila stared at the rain on the window. That night she switched off the clips and slept for nine hours.

qa.q: How many easy passes did Leila drop on Thursday?
qa.a: Leila dropped three easy passes.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when she deleted the message about Nkechi?
qa.a: Leila felt ashamed, recognising that her fixation was pushing her toward sabotage.

qa.q: What small step did Leila take to break the fixation?
qa.a: She switched off Nkechi's clips and slept, putting her energy back into her own game and rest.

qa.q: How might Nkechi see Leila's constant watching at practice?
qa.a: Nkechi might feel uncomfortable and watched, without knowing why Leila seems so tense around her.

grounding: Shows a teen obsessed with beating a rival, close to spreading a rumour, who sees the fixation is draining her own focus.

passage: The video went up at 8 p.m.: Avni singing on the Ganesh festival stage in their small town, her voice cracking on the high note. By nine the class group had eighty messages. Crying-laughing faces. "Donkey solo." Someone turned it into a sticker. Farhan's thumb hovered. One laughing face and he'd fit in. Staying quiet was easier still. He remembered Avni lending him her notes when he had typhoid. He typed in the group, "Guys, enough. She was brave to get on stage." Two people replied with eye-rolls. Then he opened a private chat. "Hey, I saw the group. That's not ok. You ok?" Avni replied after a long minute: "thanks. I thought everyone was laughing." Farhan showed the group to his mother, who messaged the class teacher that night; by morning the sticker was gone.

qa.q: When did the video go up?
qa.a: The video went up at 8 p.m.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling as his thumb hovered?
qa.a: Farhan felt torn and uneasy, tempted to fit in by laughing but remembering Avni's kindness with the notes.

qa.q: Which choices did Farhan make, and why do they matter?
qa.a: He spoke up once in the group, messaged Avni privately and showed his mother, so Avni knew someone was with her and an adult could step in.

qa.q: How might Avni feel reading Farhan's private message?
qa.a: Avni likely feels a little less alone and relieved, since she thought everyone was laughing.

grounding: Illustrates a teen watching a group-chat pile-on, choosing to defend the target and message her privately rather than join or stay silent.

passage: In Chicago, the basketball team chat blew up after Jamal missed the final free throw. "Choke artist." "Brick Jamal." Somebody posted a slowed-down clip with sad music. Javier lay on his bed reading it, stomach tight. He wasn't brave enough to take on the whole team in public; the captain had started it. But he opened a private message. "Hey man. The chat is out of line. You carried us in the third quarter. Want me to tell Coach Rivera?" The reply came fast. "yeah. I can't make it stop." Javier emailed Coach Rivera that night with screenshots. At 10 p.m. the coach posted in the chat: "Clip comes down now. We win and lose as a team. Meeting tomorrow at 7."

qa.q: Who started the pile-on in the chat?
qa.a: The captain had started it.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling as he read the chat?
qa.a: Javier felt uneasy and afraid, with a tight stomach, not brave enough to challenge the captain in public.

qa.q: What was the courageous choice Javier made, and why did it help?
qa.a: He messaged Jamal privately and, with Jamal's okay, sent screenshots to Coach Rivera, so an adult stopped the pile-on that night.

qa.q: How might Jamal see Javier's private message?
qa.a: Jamal probably feels relieved and less alone, since he couldn't make the chat stop by himself.

grounding: Shows a teen who cannot face a public pile-on still messaging the target privately and bringing in the coach.

passage: I'm Manjula, and two weeks ago I got into a pointless fight with a stranger online. I'd posted my drawing of a heron on an art forum. Someone called "realart_only" commented: "Kids shouldn't post trash. Delete this." My face went hot. At midnight I typed three long replies, each ruder than the last. The stranger kept going, and the more I answered, the more they laughed. I couldn't sleep. Next morning my friend Sabina looked at my phone and said, "You're feeding them. They want you angry." She showed me how to mute and block. I did both, and then I tried something new: I waited a whole day before posting anything. My next heron got twelve kind comments. I read them after a good night's sleep.

qa.q: What did "realart_only" comment on the heron drawing?
qa.a: The comment said, "Kids shouldn't post trash. Delete this."

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling while typing the midnight replies?
qa.a: Manjula felt hurt and angry, with a hot face, and got more heated with each reply.

qa.q: Which steps helped Manjula, and why?
qa.a: Muting and blocking cut off the troll, and waiting a day before posting stopped Manjula reacting in anger.

qa.q: How did the stranger likely see Manjula's angry replies?
qa.a: The stranger probably enjoyed them, since the more Manjula answered, the more they laughed.

grounding: Illustrates a teen baited by an online stranger into heated replies, then learning not to feed trolls, to mute and block, and to sleep first.

passage:
Warden's log, boys' hostel, Tuesday night (Preeti, night warden)
12:40 a.m. On my round I found Hrithik, Class 11, sitting up under his blanket, phone glowing, jaw clenched. He said a stranger on a cricket forum had called his home state "full of idiots" and he was "destroying" them. He had sent fifteen replies. I asked him to read me the last one aloud. He stopped halfway and went red. We talked about trolls wanting a reaction. He muted the thread, blocked the account, and agreed to leave any reply until after breakfast. Lights off at 1:05.
At breakfast he said he no longer wanted to reply at all. I will raise online baiting at Friday's house meeting.

qa.q: How many replies had Hrithik sent?
qa.a: Hrithik had sent fifteen replies.

qa.q: What does Hrithik going red while reading his reply aloud suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Hrithik felt embarrassed, hearing how angry and harsh the reply sounded outside his head.

qa.q: What did Preeti help Hrithik do?
qa.a: Preeti helped him see that trolls want a reaction; then he muted the thread, blocked the account and waited until after breakfast.

qa.q: How might the online stranger have felt reading fifteen replies?
qa.a: The stranger likely felt pleased, since getting Hrithik angry was the point of the insult.

grounding: Shows a teen baited by an online stranger late at night, and a warden helping him mute, block and sleep before responding.

passage: At the Sunday youth circle in the temple community hall, the priest, Acharya-ji, asked if anyone had questions about the week's reading. Deepika's hand went up before she could stop it. "If God is kind, why did my Nani suffer so much before she died?" The room went still. Her cheeks burned; she felt she had said something terrible in a holy place. Hrithik, beside her, stared at his knees. Acharya-ji didn't frown. "That question is older than this temple, Deepika. Many saints asked it." He gave her two short passages to read and said, "Come back with more questions, not fewer." Walking out, Hrithik whispered, "I wonder about that too." Deepika's guilt loosened a little. She had no answer yet, but she had permission to keep looking.

qa.q: What did Deepika ask Acharya-ji?
qa.a: Deepika asked, "If God is kind, why did my Nani suffer so much before she died?"

qa.q: Why did Deepika's cheeks burn after asking?
qa.a: Deepika felt guilty and embarrassed, as if doubting in a holy place was terrible.

qa.q: What made Acharya-ji's response helpful?
qa.a: He treated the question as old and normal, gave passages to read and invited more questions, so doubt became part of searching.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Deepika's question?
qa.a: Hrithik seems relieved that someone said it aloud, since he wonders about it too.

grounding: Illustrates a teen asking a hard question about faith, feeling guilty, and being shown that honest doubt is part of building conviction.

passage:
Dear Kishore Mama,

You always said I could ask you anything, so here goes. At Durga Puja this year I stood in the pandal and didn't feel what everyone else seemed to feel. I did the anjali with Ma, but my head was full of questions: how do we know any of it is true? Why do different religions say different things? Then I felt terrible, like I was betraying Ma and Thakuma, who pray every morning.

I haven't told them. I don't want to hurt anyone, but I don't want to pretend either. You read so much philosophy. Did you ever doubt? What did you do with it?

Please don't tell Ma yet.

Your nephew,
Anirban

qa.q: What did Anirban do with Ma at Durga Puja?
qa.a: Anirban did the anjali with Ma.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling after the questions came up in the pandal?
qa.a: Anirban felt guilty and confused, as if doubting meant betraying Ma and Thakuma.

qa.q: How might Kishore Mama help Anirban with the doubt?
qa.a: He could share his own experience of doubt, reassure Anirban that questioning is normal, and suggest reading and, in time, talking honestly with Ma.

qa.q: How might Ma feel if she later learned of Anirban's doubts?
qa.a: Ma might feel worried or sad at first, but could also be touched that Anirban tried so hard not to hurt her.

grounding: Shows a teen questioning the family faith, feeling guilty about it, and reaching out honestly instead of pretending.

passage: I'm Ankita, Aditi's younger sister. Since the board exams started, Aditi has been getting up at five to sit by the tulsi plant with her eyes closed for twenty minutes. She used to snap at everyone before exams; this year she's calmer, and she even helped me with my Hindi. But last week I heard her tell our cousin, "You don't even pray, no wonder you're stressed," in a voice I didn't like. Our cousin went quiet. That night I saw Aditi sitting on her bed, frowning at her prayer book. The next morning she went to our cousin's room and said something I couldn't hear, and they both laughed. I don't know what she prays about, but she seems steadier, and kinder again.

qa.q: What time has Aditi been getting up since the exams started?
qa.a: Aditi has been getting up at five.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling as she frowned at her prayer book that night?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, sensing her words to the cousin didn't match what her prayer was meant to make her.

qa.q: What does Aditi's morning visit to the cousin show about devotion?
qa.a: It suggests she chose to repair the hurt, letting her practice make her kinder rather than superior.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt when Aditi said "You don't even pray"?
qa.a: The cousin likely felt judged and hurt, which is why they went quiet.

grounding: Illustrates, through a sister's eyes, a teen steadied by daily prayer who catches herself looking down on others and turns back to kindness.

passage:
First Sunday: Mahima started helping at the gurdwara langar near her Ludhiana home, rolling rotis beside women three times her age. By noon her arms ached, but she felt quiet inside for the first time since board-exam stress began.
Third Sunday: She told Aparna, "You should come. Unless you're too busy with your phone." Aparna's face closed. Mahima felt a flicker of superiority, then an odd shame; the aunties at the langar had never once made her feel small.
Fifth Sunday: Mahima had texted Aparna, "Sorry for that. No pressure. I just like it there." Aparna came, burned her first roti, and laughed. Mahima showed her how to flip it, the way the aunties had shown her.

qa.q: Where did Mahima start helping on Sundays?
qa.a: Mahima started helping at the gurdwara langar near her Ludhiana home.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling on the third Sunday after her comment to Aparna?
qa.a: Mahima felt a flicker of superiority and then shame, since the aunties had never made her feel small.

qa.q: How did Mahima's devotion become kinder in the end?
qa.a: She apologised to Aparna without pressure and taught her to flip rotis, sharing the service instead of using it to judge.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when told she was too busy with her phone?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt judged and shut out, which is why her face closed.

grounding: Shows a teen steadied by service at the langar, catching a moment of superiority and choosing kindness instead.
